title: The annoying sister (Manuscript C)
hookLine: speak up or smile? two old works of mercy, and the one Thérèse chose for the nun who grated on her
tomorrow: dirty water in your face, again and again. now what?

cards: Every group chat has one. The person who corrects everyone's spelling, answers every joke with a fact, takes the last of the coffee and never makes more. Not cruel.

Just grating, every single day. Thérèse had one, in a small convent where you can't mute anybody. In Manuscript C, she describes a sister who displeased her in everything: her ways, her words, her character.
She never gives her name. So what do you do with a person like that? The Church's old lists hold two honest answers.

teach.b: Among the spiritual works of mercy, Catholics list both: admonish the sinner, and bear wrongs patiently.
Here's the best case for speaking up. Silence can be fake. A smile over gritted teeth can feel like a lie, and the other person never learns why people drift away from her.
A true word, said kindly, might be the help nobody gave her. That's a real Catholic view. Now the other side.
With this sister, there was no sin to correct. It was just her. So Thérèse chose the second work.
She prayed for her. She did her small favors.

When a sharp reply rose up, she gave her warmest smile and changed the subject. Some days, she admits, the struggle was too strong, so she ran, like a deserter, and she tells that with a straight face.
One day the sister asked her: what is it that draws you to me so much? Thérèse's answer, in her notebook: she was looking at Jesus hidden deep in that soul.
Behind it is Christ's command at the Last Supper, in the Douay-Rheims: "A new commandment I give unto you: That you love one another, as I have loved you."
For Thérèse, that love isn't a warm feeling. It's a choice, made toward the one you'd never pick. Both views agree on that much.
They differ on what love says out loud.

how: Catholics often tell this story from Manuscript C as a picture of Thérèse's little way: charity shown in small, ordinary choices toward people who are hard to love.

o: Thérèse's real sister, who teased her growing up
the nun who grated on Thérèse, and got her kindest smile
a nun who bullied Thérèse until she nearly left

games.q: the sister who grated — tap the pairs.
p: her warmest, for the hardest one
love as I have loved you

s: Thérèse got along easily with everyone in her convent
she describes a sister who displeased her in everything: ways, words, character.
admonishing and bearing wrongs patiently are both works of mercy
both are on the old list; with this sister Thérèse chose the second.
the sister could tell Thérèse found her hard to bear
she asked what drew Thérèse to her so much.

games.q: your grandpa tells the same fishing story at every dinner, and your sister groans out loud. admonish, or bear patiently: which fits this one?
o: bear it with a smile: nothing wrong is happening, it's just him.
admonish him kindly, so he learns he's repeating himself.
slip away from the table whenever the story starts.
games.why: admonishing is for real wrongs, and a repeated story isn't one. that's the smile, like Thérèse's. (she admits she slipped away some days too, but as a last resort.)

practice: Sit tall and let your face go soft: jaw, eyes, forehead. Bring to mind the person who grates on you most, and let the corners of your mouth lift, just a little, while you hold them there. If you pray, you can pray for them by name.
